beats.narration_text: Feature catalogue. A scene whose purpose is to show what a system can do. Not a playable game. Not tested headlessly. A set of configured effects you read and port from. Compatibility renderer. The renderer that runs on the widest hardware: mobile, embedded, older GPUs. Particle trails and SDF collision are unsupported. The class reference confirms. Draw pass. One of a particle node's material slots. The process material decides where particles go. The draw pass decides what each particle looks like: its texture, blend mode, and shading. Tres file. A Godot resource file stored separately from any node, with a dot-tres extension. A particle draw material in its own file can be shared and referenced by multiple effects. FRICTIONAL dot MD. The human's record of a build: what the agent did, what you ran, what failed, what you saw on screen. The only evidence that an effect looks like anything.

beats.narration_text: The godot-demo-projects repository, pinned at commit a3b5c113, has a scene called 2d/particles. Seventeen GPU Particles 2D nodes. One scene. Mobile renderer. Each node is one pattern: a fountain, a fire, a trail, sparks, smoke, a galaxy, a flame thrower. There is no Walker adaptation. No test harness. No game logic. Every effect in it is readable. Open the .tscn file, trace each node's process material, port it to your project. That catalogue is the fastest particle library a Godot project can have.

beats.narration_text: The same commit has 3d/particles. Forward Plus renderer. This scene exercises three GPU features that the 2D catalog does not show in action: trails, SDF collision, and attractors. Trail enabled: GPU nodes only. CPUParticles3D has no trail enabled at all, and Compatibility does not support it even on GPU nodes. SDF collision: particles that bounce off scene geometry. Needs depth rendering — Forward Plus or Mobile only. Attractors: velocity fields that shape all live particles. Everything in this catalog that uses trails, SDF collision, or sub-emitters requires Forward Plus or Mobile. On Compatibility, those effects don't run.

beats.narration_text: When you port an effect from a catalog, the three-part frame tells you what to carry. Emission: amount, lifetime, explosiveness, one-shot. These are on the node. They port directly between CPU and GPU. Process: velocity, gravity, spread, turbulence, attractors, sub-emitters. On GPU nodes these live in the Particle Process Material. On CPU nodes they are node properties. Sub-emitters and particle shaders are GPU only. Draw: the texture, the material, the blend mode. This is the draw pass. It is independent of whether you use CPU or GPU. A tres file for the draw half ports anywhere. The catalog tells you what effect exists. The frame tells you what to carry when you move it.

beats.narration_text: The Godot editor converts a CPU Particles 2D to GPU Particles 2D with one button in the 2D toolbar. The 3D toolbar has the same option. What the conversion preserves: amount, lifetime, explosiveness, one-shot, local-coords, fixed FPS, and the timing model. The emission settings — spread, velocity range, gravity, lifetime randomness — move from node properties into a new Particle Process Material. What you gain: the GPU node now has sub-emitter, trail enabled, and a process material that supports turbulence, attractors, and collision. CPU to GPU is additive. You keep the effect and gain features.

beats.narration_text: Converting from GPU Particles 2D to CPU Particles 2D is a one-way degradation. Most emission settings survive. The process material becomes node properties for the settings that have equivalents. What cannot survive: sub-emitter. Trail enabled. Particle shaders. The process material's turbulence, attractors, and collision. If an effect uses any of those, converting to CPU changes the effect. A particle shader becomes a plain process material with whatever settings can be matched. A sub-emitter chain disappears entirely. GPU to CPU is not the same effect on different hardware. It is a simpler effect on wider hardware.

beats.narration_text: Every effect in your library should carry a renderer tag. Compatibility: the widest target. Particle trails: unsupported. SDF collision: unsupported. emit-particle, the scripted spawn method on GPU nodes: Forward Plus or Mobile only. Effects built for Compatibility cannot use any of those. Mobile: modern devices. Trails work. SDF collision works. emit-particle works. Forward Plus: the full feature set. Everything works, including the 3D demo's sub-emitter chains and attractor fields. A library that does not tag renderer requirements will fail on the wrong machine without a clear error.

beats.narration_text: Act three. Cross-engine map.

lecture.about: Act divider

shot.visual_intent: Act divider

beats.narration_text: Unity's two particle systems map directly to Godot's two families. The Built-in Particle System is CPU-simulated. Its scene files serialise as YAML. An agent can read them, diff them, edit them. The sub-emitter mechanism is the Sub Emitters module. The equivalent of Godot's finished signal is OnParticleSystemStopped. The Visual Effect Graph is GPU-simulated. Its assets are dot-vfx files. VFX Graph assets are not described as text-diffable by Unity's documentation. An agent cannot inspect the emitter stack the way it reads a .tscn. For the death burst: one-shot maps to Looping off; amount plus explosiveness one maps to Spawn Burst Instantaneous; finished maps to OnParticleSystemStopped.

lecture.about: Unity Built-in (CPU, YAML readable) vs VFX Graph (GPU, binary) vs Godot

beats.narration_text: Unreal Engine's Niagara is one particle system with CPU and GPU selectable per emitter via the Sim Target setting. The one-shot burst: Emitter State with Loop Behavior Once — Godot's one-shot. Spawn Burst Instantaneous with a count of 32 — Godot's amount with explosiveness one. The equivalent of finished is UNiagara Component dot OnSystemFinished. Niagara systems are stored as dot-uasset files. Epic's own source-control documentation confirms they are binary and cannot be opened as text or merged with text tools. An agent can write the C++ that spawns the system and can drive the editor with the Python Editor Script Plugin. Niagara events — the sub-emitter mechanism — work on CPU simulation only. Godot's sub-emitters are GPU only. The two are mirrors of each other.

beats.narration_text: The practical difference for agent work is file format. A Godot scene file is plain text. A particle node's configuration, its process material, and its sub-emitter reference are all visible in the .tscn. The draw material is in a .tres. An agent can read both, run a diff, and verify specific properties without running the game. Unity prefabs are YAML — the Built-in system is readable. VFX Graph assets are not. Unreal's .uasset is binary for all visual content. That is why the Chapter 9 agent could confirm that DeathBurst is a child of Main, that its process material has particle-flag-disable-z set to true, and that its texture is a GradientTexture2D — from the scene file, before a single test ran. No other engine in this course gives agents that reach into a particle configuration.

beats.narration_text: Walker-3d-platformer's particle-material-dot-tres is a Standard Material 3D in its own file, with four flags: additive blend mode, unshaded shading mode, particle billboard mode, proximity fade enabled. The coin burst, the enemy explosion, and the bullet glow all reference the same file via material-override. Change additive to alpha-blend for smoke: one edit, three effects update. The draw half is stable. For a given art style, the blend mode and billboard mode do not change between effects. What changes is the process material — velocity, spread, lifetime randomness. Keep the draw half in a named file. Reference it everywhere.

beats.narration_text: A practical VFX library entry has five fields. Name: what the effect is called in this project. Renderer: Compatibility, Mobile, or Forward Plus. The minimum needed to run the effect. Node type: CPU or GPU. CPU runs anywhere within its renderer; GPU gains sub-emitters, trails, and shaders. Draw material: the tres file this effect uses for its draw pass. Shared effects point to the same file. Test status: what the headless test establishes. Not what it proves visually — what it checks in state. Build one card per effect before you build the effect. It answers the questions your prompt needs to ask.

beats.narration_text: Here is particle-material-dot-tres as the Godot editor shows it. A Standard Material 3D. Four flags. Blend mode: additive. Shading mode: unshaded. Billboard mode: particle. beats.narration_text: Here is what a practical library gives you. The Godot catalog: 2D has 17 GPU effects on Mobile. 3D has trails, attractors, SDF collision, and sub-emitters on Forward Plus. Both are plain text .tscn files. Neither has a Walker adaptation. Conversion: CPU to GPU gains a process material and all GPU features. GPU to CPU loses sub-emitters, trails, and shaders. Compatibility drops trails and SDF collision entirely. Tag every library effect with its renderer requirement. Cross-engine: Godot's text scene format gives agents the most reach. Unity's Built-in YAML is readable. VFX Graph and Niagara assets are binary. Agents can configure the spawn call in code; they cannot inspect the full effect stack from a file. The tres pattern: one draw material file, shared by multiple effects. Change the look once. Port the file to the next project.
